title: When Do FY 2027 ICD-10-PCS Updates
excerpt: FY 2027 ICD-10-PCS updates take effect October 1, 2026. Learn about new, deleted and revised procedure codes, implementation requirements and coding guidelines.
content:
If you work with inpatient coding, the FY 2027 ICD-10-PCS effective date is an important deadline. The new ICD-10-PCS code set becomes effective for applicable discharges beginning October 1, 2026.

CMS has released the FY 2027 ICD-10-PCS code tables, index, conversion table, addendum, official coding guidelines and version update materials. CMS currently identifies the FY 2027 PCS files as applicable to discharges from October 1, 2026 through March 31, 2027.

FY 2027 ICD-10-PCS at a Glance

Update Type Count FY 2027 Detail New Codes 101 Includes new technology and standard-table additions Deleted Codes 38 Codes scheduled for removal Revised Codes 3 Title revisions Effective Date — October 1, 2026 The release represents a significant increase in new PCS codes compared with FY 2026, making advance preparation especially important for inpatient coding departments.

What Is New in FY 2027?

One of the major areas receiving attention is the New Technology Group 12 additions. These codes address newer technologies and procedures that require specific representation within the ICD-10-PCS system.

Examples included in the FY 2027 materials include procedures involving a leadless neurostimulator generator, transcatheter septal scoring and an allogeneic stem-cell-derived islet cell therapy.

There are also standard-table additions, covering procedures across different body systems and approaches. Examples include certain aortic valve procedures, transfusion-related procedures and retinal vessel imaging.

Because ICD-10-PCS codes are built from multiple characters representing specific components of a procedure, coders should avoid selecting codes based only on a familiar procedure name. The complete operative documentation and PCS definitions remain essential.

Why Are 38 Codes Being Deleted?

The FY 2027 update also removes 38 existing codes. Some are associated with technology-specific procedure coding cohorts that have reached their scheduled sunset.

This is important because a deleted code does not necessarily mean that the underlying procedure is no longer performed. In some situations, the procedure may instead be represented through existing standard PCS tables.

Therefore, inpatient coding teams should review deleted codes alongside the updated tables and guidelines instead of simply removing them from internal references.

FY 2026 vs FY 2027

Fiscal Year New Deleted Revised Effective FY 2026 38 43 1 Oct. 1, 2025 FY 2027 101 38 3 Oct. 1, 2026 CMS has also published FY 2027 MS-DRG Version 44 materials, including updated Medicare Code Edits and grouper-related files. This is important because PCS changes can interact with inpatient grouping and claim-processing workflows.

Recent Professional Discussion: Implementation Is the Bigger Issue

Recent coding and RCM discussions surrounding the FY 2027 release have increasingly focused on implementation rather than simply memorizing new codes.

For hospitals and inpatient coding teams, an annual PCS update can affect encoders, code libraries, education materials, internal references, auditing processes and claim-edit workflows.

Experienced medical coding support can also help organizations review documentation and maintain accurate coding workflows as requirements change.

That means organizations should test their systems before October 1 instead of waiting until the first production claim encounters a problem.

Another important point is that ICD-10-PCS should be reviewed alongside related MS-DRG and Medicare Code Edit updates. CMS has already made FY 2027 Version 44 materials available, including software and documentation for the updated grouping environment.

FY 2027 PCS Preparation Checklist

Before implementation, inpatient coding departments should:

  • Download the official FY 2027 PCS files.
  • Review all new and deleted codes.
  • Study revised code titles.
  • Review the updated PCS guidelines.
  • Update encoder software.
  • Update internal procedure references.
  • Review technology-specific procedures.
  • Test the updated code set with sample cases.
  • Confirm MS-DRG grouper and edit updates.
  • Educate coding and HIM staff.
  • Monitor post-implementation coding questions and claim edits.

AHIMA's 2027 educational materials also reflect the updated PCS code set and guidelines, including expanded examples and coverage of trauma procedures.

Effective Date: What You Need to Remember

The key implementation date is October 1, 2026. Organizations should use the FY 2027 ICD-10-PCS materials for applicable inpatient discharges beginning on that date, while following the specific CMS instructions for the applicable reporting period.

Frequently Asked Question

When do FY 2027 ICD-10-PCS updates go into effect?

The FY 2027 ICD-10-PCS update becomes effective October 1, 2026 for applicable inpatient discharges.

The safest implementation strategy is to use the official CMS code files, guidelines, conversion materials and related MS-DRG documentation rather than relying on older code lists or unofficial summaries.

title: ICD-10 Changes 2027:
excerpt: Explore FY 2027 ICD-10-CM updates effective October 1, 2026, including new, deleted and revised codes, major changes, implementation tips and coding guidance.
content:
The FY 2027 release contains 190 new codes, 30 deleted codes and four revised descriptors according to the release analysis provided for this update.

While the number of new codes is lower than the previous fiscal year, the practical issue for coding teams is not simply the number of additions. The important question is whether the changes affect the diagnoses and specialties handled by a particular organization.

Major Areas to Watch

Several FY 2027 changes deserve particular attention during preparation.

Injury and poisoning: This chapter contains a substantial portion of the new and deleted codes, making it especially important for organizations handling trauma, toxic effects and related encounters.

Pregnancy-related coding: New specificity in pregnancy-related diagnoses means coders should review documentation requirements carefully rather than relying on previously used unspecified options.

Odontogenic sinusitis: New coding detail provides additional specificity for this condition.

Plantar fasciitis: Site-specific coding changes are relevant for orthopedic and musculoskeletal practices and may require updates to code-selection workflows.

Cardiomyopathy and BMI: Changes affecting these areas reinforce the need to review both diagnosis selection and documentation workflows.

CMS has also made the official FY 2027 conversion table, code descriptions, addendum and coding guidelines available for implementation planning.

Why the 2027 Update Matters for RCM

Recent professional discussions around the upcoming code-set change have focused on a practical issue: coding changes can create downstream revenue-cycle problems when systems and workflows are not updated together.

A deleted or replaced diagnosis code may appear harmless during code selection, but it can become a problem if an EHR preference list, encoder, superbill, billing software or internal coding reference still contains outdated information.

That is why implementation should involve more than simply downloading the new code list.

Before October 1, organizations should review:

EHR diagnosis favorites

Superbill templates

Encoder and coding software

Billing and practice-management systems

Clinical documentation workflows

Payer-specific medical-necessity requirements

Internal coding policies

Claim-edit and denial workflows

What Should Happen to Deleted Codes?

The 30 deleted codes should be reviewed before the effective date. A practical approach is to identify where those codes currently appear and determine whether a replacement, more specific code or updated documentation is required.

CMS provides a FY 2027 conversion table, which can support this review. However, coders should not automatically substitute a new code simply because it appears to be similar. The official guidelines, tabular instructions and clinical documentation should still be reviewed.

Recent Industry Discussion: Beyond the Code List

One recurring theme in recent healthcare coding and RCM discussions is that annual ICD-10 updates should be treated as a workflow-change project, not merely a coding-reference update.

This is particularly relevant when organizations use automated claim edits, electronic superbills, customized diagnosis lists or multiple billing systems. A code may be technically available in the new code set while still being missing from an organization's operational workflow.

The FY 2027 update also arrives alongside continuing changes to Medicare coverage and other coding-related policies. CMS has published additional October 2026 ICD-10 revisions affecting National Coverage Determinations, demonstrating why coding teams should review related payer and coverage updates rather than examining diagnosis codes in isolation.

FY 2027 ICD-10-CM Implementation Checklist

Before October 1, 2026:

Download the official FY 2027 code files.

Review new, deleted and revised codes.

Run the conversion table against frequently used codes.

Update EHR and billing-system code libraries.

Review superbills and diagnosis favorites.

Educate coding and billing staff.

Test claims before the effective date.

Monitor denials after implementation.

Review payer-specific requirements.

Document recurring issues for corrective action.

title: Medicaid Income Rules 2026: Caregiving, Self-Employment & Work Requirements
excerpt: Learn how Medicaid income rules in 2026 may affect caregivers, self-employed workers and part-time employees, including income reporting and upcoming work requirements.
content:
Medicaid eligibility can become complicated when your income changes, you start working part-time, receive payments for caregiving, or earn money through self-employment.

In 2026, these issues are receiving more attention because Medicaid eligibility and work requirements are changing. However, Medicaid rules are not the same in every state, and the new federal community engagement requirements are generally scheduled to begin on January 1, 2027, unless a state implements them earlier.

Here are some common situations that can help explain how Medicaid income rules in 2026 may affect caregivers, workers, freelancers and other Medicaid beneficiaries.

1. Can a Temporary Increase in Income Cause Me to Lose Medicaid?

This is a common concern for people whose income changes from month to month.

For example, consider a family caregiver who receives payment for providing care to a parent. If the parent's care needs suddenly increase, the caregiver may earn considerably more in one month than usual.

The question is simple:

If my income increases for one or two months, will I automatically lose Medicaid for the entire year?

There is no single answer for every Medicaid beneficiary. Eligibility depends on the person's Medicaid category, household circumstances and state rules.

For many adults covered under MAGI-based Medicaid, income is an important part of determining eligibility. MAGI-based rules apply to many children, pregnant women, parents and adults, while other Medicaid programs use different financial eligibility rules.

A temporary increase in income should therefore not automatically be treated as a one-year disqualification from Medicaid. If your circumstances change, your state Medicaid agency may reassess your eligibility under the rules that apply to your particular program.

This situation is sometimes referred to as a Medicaid income cliff, particularly when a small increase in income causes someone to exceed an applicable eligibility limit.

The important point is to report income changes according to your state's requirements. Do not stop reporting income simply because you expect your earnings to decrease again.

Keeping records of what you earned can also make it easier to explain temporary changes in income.

2. Do Payments From Family Members Count as Medicaid Income?

Another common situation involves financial help from family members.

Suppose someone leaves a part-time job and a family member begins helping with rent, groceries or other household expenses.

Does every dollar of family assistance automatically count as Medicaid income?

Not necessarily.

The answer depends on what the payment actually represents and which Medicaid eligibility rules apply.

Money received as wages or payment for services is different from a genuine gift or other type of financial assistance. Medicaid also uses different financial rules depending on the beneficiary's eligibility category.

For that reason, it is risky to assume that every payment from a family member must be treated as earned income—or that none of it needs to be reported.

If you receive regular financial support, explain the situation to your Medicaid agency and ask how the payment should be reported.

Do not rely solely on advice from an online forum when the classification of a payment could affect your health coverage.

3. Can Self-Employment Count Toward Medicaid Work Requirements?

Self-employed workers and freelancers may have another important question:

If I work for myself, can those hours count toward a Medicaid work requirement?

Under the federal community engagement provisions, applicable individuals may satisfy the requirement through qualifying work, community service, work programs or education.

The standard is generally 80 hours per month, although there are alternative ways to meet the requirement and exemptions may apply.

Importantly, the federal community engagement requirement is generally scheduled to begin on January 1, 2027, unless a state implements it earlier.

For applicable individuals, qualifying work can include employment and certain self-employment activities. Medicaid guidance also provides an earnings-based pathway tied to the federal minimum wage.

For people who are self-employed, keeping accurate records can therefore become important.

Useful documentation may include:

  • Invoices
  • Business payment records
  • Contracts
  • Business bank statements
  • Client records
  • Work logs or timesheets
  • Other records showing the work performed

The exact documentation requirements may vary by state and program.

It is also important to distinguish between self-employment income and work hours. Having income from a business does not necessarily mean that every hour spent on the business will automatically satisfy a particular state's verification requirements.

Medicaid Payments Received by Family Caregivers

Caregiving payments require special attention because not every caregiving payment is treated the same way for tax or Medicaid purposes.

Certain Medicaid waiver payments may qualify for special federal income-tax treatment when specific requirements are met. For example, some payments may be excluded from federal gross income when a caregiver provides care to an eligible individual living in the caregiver's home.

Other caregiving payments may be taxable or treated differently depending on the circumstances.

Family caregivers can also have different employment and tax classifications depending on who pays them, who employs them and how the caregiving arrangement is structured.

For this reason, do not assume that every payment described as a Medicaid caregiving payment automatically counts—or does not count—as income for Medicaid eligibility.

The source of the payment, Medicaid program, living arrangement and eligibility category can all matter.

If you receive caregiving payments and are concerned about Medicaid eligibility, check with your state Medicaid agency and, where appropriate, a qualified tax professional.

What Should You Do When Your Income Changes?

If you receive Medicaid and your income changes, the safest approach is to keep accurate records and follow your state's reporting instructions.

1. Report Changes on Time

Medicaid beneficiaries are responsible for providing accurate information and reporting changes that may affect eligibility.

The specific reporting deadline can vary by state and by the type of change.

Do not assume that a specific deadline, such as 10 days, applies everywhere. Check your state's Medicaid instructions for the correct reporting requirements.

2. Keep Monthly Income Records

If your income changes frequently, maintain a simple record of:

  • Gross income
  • Paychecks
  • Business income
  • Self-employment payments
  • Caregiving payments
  • Hours worked
  • Supporting documents

Good records can make it easier to respond if Medicaid requests income verification.

3. Understand Your Medicaid Eligibility Category

Medicaid does not use one single income rule for everyone.

MAGI-based Medicaid covers many children, pregnant women, parents and adults, while other Medicaid eligibility pathways can use different financial methodologies.

Knowing which Medicaid category you are enrolled in can make a significant difference when evaluating an income change.

4. Check Your State's Rules

Medicaid is administered by individual states within federal requirements. As a result, procedures for reporting income, verifying work activity and determining eligibility can differ.

If you are unsure how a particular payment or income change should be reported, contact your state Medicaid agency or a qualified healthcare navigator.

What Happens If You Lose Medicaid Coverage?

Losing Medicaid does not necessarily mean that you have to remain uninsured until the next annual enrollment period.

Depending on the circumstances, losing Medicaid coverage may qualify you for a Special Enrollment Period to enroll in a Marketplace health insurance plan.

If you receive a notice that your Medicaid coverage is ending, check your Marketplace eligibility and enrollment options as soon as possible.

Key Takeaways

The most important things to understand about Medicaid income rules in 2026 are:

1.     A temporary increase in income does not automatically mean a one-year loss of Medicaid. The effect depends on your Medicaid eligibility category and state rules.

2.     Not every payment from a family member is automatically earned income. The purpose and nature of the payment matter.

3.     Self-employment may qualify as work activity when community engagement requirements apply. However, the new federal requirement is generally scheduled for 2027, and states may implement it earlier.

4.     Keep records of income and work activity. Invoices, payment records and timesheets can help if your state requests verification.

5.     Caregiving payments may receive special tax treatment in certain circumstances. Do not assume that all caregiving payments are treated the same way.

6.     Medicaid rules vary by state and eligibility category. Always verify your specific situation with your state Medicaid agency or a qualified healthcare navigator.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Medicaid Check Income Every Month?

There is no single income-check procedure that applies to every Medicaid beneficiary.

The way income is evaluated depends on the Medicaid eligibility category and state. Many adults qualify under MAGI-based rules, while other Medicaid programs use different financial methodologies.

If your income changes, follow your state's reporting and renewal instructions rather than assuming that your eligibility will be reviewed in the same way as someone in another Medicaid program.

Can Caregiving Payments Affect Medicaid Eligibility?

They can, depending on the type of payment and the Medicaid eligibility rules that apply to you.

Certain Medicaid waiver payments may receive special treatment for federal income-tax purposes under specific circumstances. This does not mean that every caregiving payment is automatically excluded from Medicaid income calculations.

If you receive payment for caregiving, check how that particular payment is treated under your Medicaid program.

Can Self-Employment Count Toward the 80-Hour Medicaid Requirement?

Self-employment can qualify as work activity when the applicable community engagement requirements are in effect and the activity meets the relevant rules.

The federal standard is generally 80 hours per month, but the new federal requirement is generally scheduled to begin on January 1, 2027, unless a state implements it earlier.

Individuals should also check whether an exemption or alternative pathway applies to their situation.

Do I Have to Report Financial Help From My Family?

It depends on the type of financial help and the Medicaid rules that apply to you.

Payment received for services is different from a genuine gift. Because the treatment can vary depending on the Medicaid eligibility category, it is best to ask your state Medicaid agency how the specific payment should be reported.

What If I Lose Medicaid Because My Income Increases?

You may have other health coverage options.

Depending on the circumstances, losing Medicaid eligibility can trigger a Special Enrollment Period for Marketplace coverage.

If you receive a notice that your Medicaid coverage is ending, check your Marketplace options promptly rather than waiting for the next annual enrollment period.

Final Thoughts

Changes in income do not always have a simple yes-or-no effect on Medicaid coverage.

The outcome can depend on your state, Medicaid eligibility category, household circumstances and the type of income you receive.

If you are a caregiver, freelancer, self-employed worker or part-time employee, keep your income and work records organized and follow your state's reporting requirements.

When you are unsure how a particular payment or income change affects your coverage, contact your state Medicaid agency or a qualified healthcare navigator for guidance based on your individual circumstances.

Disclaimer: This article is for general informational purposes only and does not provide legal, tax or medical advice. Medicaid eligibility rules can vary by state, program and individual circumstances. Always verify your situation with your state Medicaid agency or a qualified professional.

title: 5 Revenue Cycle Management Trends to Watch in 2026
excerpt: Stay ahead with the latest RCM trends including AI automation, predictive analytics, and value-based care models.
content:
Top 5 Healthcare Revenue Cycle Trends Shaping 2026 — What Providers Are Actually Discussing Right Now

Healthcare revenue cycle management is no longer just about submitting claims and collecting payments. In 2026, the focus is shifting toward intelligence, prevention, automation, compliance, and patient financial experience.

For providers and billing teams, the biggest change is simple: waiting for problems to appear before fixing them is becoming increasingly inefficient. Modern RCM strategies are moving upstream—using technology and data to identify potential issues before they become denials, delays, or lost revenue.

Here are the top five healthcare revenue cycle trends shaping 2026 and influencing the conversations among RCM leaders, billing teams, healthcare organizations, and technology companies.

1. AI-Powered Claims Processing Moves From Task Automation to Intelligence

The first wave of AI in healthcare revenue cycle management focused largely on automating repetitive tasks such as routing claims, generating correspondence, and handling routine workflows.

In 2026, the focus is broader.

AI is increasingly being applied across the entire revenue cycle—from patient access and eligibility verification to coding, claims submission, denial management, reporting, and analytics.

The goal is no longer simply to automate individual tasks. Instead, organizations are looking at how AI can connect different stages of the revenue cycle and provide actionable intelligence.

One of the most important developments is predictive denial prevention. Rather than waiting for a payer to reject a claim, AI-powered systems can identify potential problems involving eligibility, authorization, coding, documentation, or other claim requirements before submission.

Intelligent coding tools can also assist coding teams by analyzing clinical documentation and suggesting potentially appropriate codes for review.

For healthcare organizations looking to implement connected workflows without building an entire technology infrastructure internally, integrated Revenue Cycle Management services can help combine automation, workflow management, and human expertise across the revenue cycle.

The broader industry conversation is also moving toward a prevention-first approach. The idea is straightforward:

The future of denial management is denial prevention.

Instead of spending most of the team's time recovering revenue after a denial, providers can use technology to address the underlying causes earlier in the process.

2. Predictive Analytics Becomes a Critical Tool for RCM Leaders

Automation can make processes faster, but predictive analytics can help organizations determine what is likely to happen next.

That distinction is becoming increasingly important for healthcare financial leaders.

Traditional RCM reporting often tells organizations what happened yesterday or last month. Predictive analytics aims to help answer questions such as:

  • Which claims are most likely to be denied?
  • Where are reimbursement delays developing?
  • Which payer trends are affecting cash flow?
  • Which accounts require immediate attention?
  • Where are authorization or eligibility problems increasing?
  • What could future revenue performance look like?

This allows RCM teams to move from reactive reporting toward more proactive decision-making.

AI and automation investments are increasingly being considered across areas such as payer analytics, coding support, eligibility, benefits verification, prior authorization, and denial management.

The result is a more data-driven revenue cycle in which leaders can identify emerging problems earlier and allocate resources where they can have the greatest operational impact.

For CFOs and RCM executives, the value is not simply having another dashboard. The real opportunity is using predictive insights to make faster decisions about cash flow, staffing, payer performance, and revenue leakage.

3. Value-Based Care Forces RCM to Connect With Clinical Data

The traditional fee-for-service model largely revolves around one central question:

Was the service documented and billed correctly?

Value-based care introduces a much broader set of requirements.

Providers increasingly need to connect financial performance with quality measures, patient outcomes, utilization, and care-delivery data.

That means RCM systems can no longer operate completely separately from clinical and operational systems.

For organizations participating in value-based arrangements, revenue depends not only on submitting accurate claims but also on demonstrating that required quality and performance measures have been achieved.

This is creating greater demand for analytics platforms capable of bringing together clinical, operational, and financial information.

Instead of looking only at whether a claim was paid, organizations can analyze questions such as:

  • Are quality requirements being met?
  • Which patient populations are generating higher costs?
  • Where are care gaps affecting financial performance?
  • How are clinical outcomes influencing reimbursement?
  • Which operational processes are creating unnecessary costs?

As value-based care continues to evolve, the connection between clinical data and revenue cycle management is likely to become increasingly important.

The conversation is gradually shifting from “Did we bill correctly?” to “Can we demonstrate the value of the care we delivered?”

4. Patient Financial Experience Is Becoming a Competitive Differentiator

Healthcare consumers increasingly expect the financial side of healthcare to be as convenient and understandable as other digital experiences.

Patients want to know what they may owe, why they owe it, and what payment options are available.

As a result, patient financial experience is becoming an increasingly important part of revenue cycle strategy.

Modern RCM initiatives are incorporating tools and processes such as:

  • Clearer financial communication
  • Digital payment options
  • Online billing portals
  • Flexible payment plans
  • Automated payment reminders
  • Pre-service financial estimates
  • Easier access to billing information

This represents an important shift in how providers view collections.

The objective is not simply to collect outstanding balances. It is also to create a financial experience that is transparent, convenient, and easier for patients to navigate.

A confusing billing process can create frustration for patients while also increasing administrative workload for provider organizations.

For this reason, patient financial experience is increasingly being considered alongside traditional RCM metrics such as collections, denial rates, days in A/R, and clean claim rates.

5. Regulatory Compliance Automation and the Payer-Provider AI Race

As AI becomes more deeply embedded in healthcare revenue cycle management, compliance and governance are becoming increasingly important.

Payers and providers are both investing in automation, but they may be using these technologies for different purposes.

Payers are using AI and automation to process claims, evaluate documentation, manage utilization, and support prior authorization and other administrative processes.

Providers, meanwhile, are increasingly using AI to improve documentation, coding accuracy, eligibility verification, authorization workflows, denial prevention, and revenue-cycle efficiency.

This creates a new challenge for healthcare organizations: technology must be fast and efficient while remaining compliant, explainable, and auditable.

That is where compliance automation becomes important.

Modern RCM technology can incorporate automated checks and workflow controls designed to identify missing documentation, authorization issues, coding inconsistencies, or other potential problems before a claim reaches the payer.

For compliance teams, the objective is not to remove humans from the process. Instead, automation can provide guardrails, documentation, auditability, and consistent workflow controls while allowing experienced professionals to handle exceptions and complex cases.

As the revenue cycle becomes more automated, organizations will need to pay greater attention to how AI decisions are governed, monitored, documented, and reviewed.

The Bottom Line

Healthcare RCM in 2026 is moving away from a purely reactive model and toward a predictive, connected, and prevention-focused approach.

The five major trends can be summarized as:

  • AI-powered RCM: Identifying and resolving potential problems before they become costly manual tasks or denials.
  • Predictive analytics: Using data to anticipate revenue, denial, and cash-flow trends.
  • Value-based care integration: Connecting financial performance with clinical outcomes and quality data.
  • Patient financial experience: Making healthcare billing more transparent, convenient, and consumer-friendly.
  • Compliance automation: Building appropriate controls and auditability into increasingly automated revenue-cycle workflows.

The important question for providers is no longer simply whether AI should be part of the revenue cycle.

The bigger question is how AI, analytics, automation, and human expertise can work together responsibly across the entire RCM process.

Organizations that focus on clean claims, early intervention, better financial visibility, connected clinical and financial data, and stronger patient experiences will be better positioned to navigate an increasingly complex healthcare revenue cycle.

In 2026, the direction of RCM is clear: less reactive work, more intelligent prevention, and greater visibility from patient access through final payment.

title: ICD-10 Coding Changes: What Providers Need to Know
excerpt: Updated ICD-10 codes for 2026 and how they impact your billing accuracy.
content:
Annual ICD-10 Updates for 2026–2027: What Every Coding Team Needs to Know

October 1 is more than just another date on the healthcare calendar.

For medical coders, billing teams, CDI professionals, and providers, it marks the start of a new ICD-10-CM fiscal year—and that means new codes, deleted codes, revised coding instructions, and changes that can affect documentation, claim accuracy, reimbursement, and compliance.

The FY 2027 ICD-10-CM code set becomes effective October 1, 2026, and remains in effect through September 30, 2027. CMS and CDC/NCHS have already released the FY 2027 files, including the code tables, addendum, conversion table, and official coding guidelines.

For coding teams, the real challenge isn't simply memorizing new code numbers.

It is making sure the right code is used for the right encounter, the documentation supports it, and every system involved in the claim is ready before October 1.

Here are the changes and preparation steps your team should have on its radar.

What Is Changing With the FY 2027 ICD-10-CM Update?

The FY 2027 update includes hundreds of changes across the code set. ACDIS reports 190 new ICD-10-CM codes, 30 deleted codes, and 4 revised codes, effective October 1, 2026.

The additions span multiple areas of medicine, including neoplasms, cardiovascular conditions, pregnancy-related diagnoses, endocrine disorders, respiratory conditions, and other clinical categories.

That matters because an annual code update can affect much more than the coding department.

It can touch:

  • Provider documentation
  • EHR diagnosis picklists
  • Encoder software
  • Charge capture
  • Claim edits
  • Medical necessity checks
  • Prior authorization workflows
  • CDI processes
  • Denial management
  • Payer-specific rules
  • Revenue-cycle reporting

In other words, ICD-10 updates are an operational change—not just a coding education exercise.

1. New Codes Bring Greater Clinical Specificity

One of the clearest themes in the FY 2027 update is greater specificity in several clinical areas.

For example, new codes include:

  • C78.31 — Secondary malignant neoplasm of larynx
  • C78.32 — Secondary malignant neoplasm of pharynx
  • C79.83 — Secondary malignant neoplasm of oral cavity

These codes become effective October 1, 2026.

For coders, greater specificity can be useful—but only when the provider's documentation actually supports that specificity.

A diagnosis documented simply as “metastatic cancer to the throat” may not provide enough information to automatically select a highly specific anatomical code.

That is why the FY 2027 update should trigger a documentation conversation between providers, coders, and CDI teams.

The question should be:

Does the documentation clearly identify the condition, site, laterality, etiology, or other detail required by the new code?

If the answer is no, the solution isn't to guess the code. The solution is to improve documentation and follow the official coding guidelines.

2. Breast Neoplasm Coding Gets an Important Instruction Change

Another change coding teams should review involves D05.-, carcinoma in situ of breast.

For FY 2027, the Excludes2 instruction relating to malignant neoplasm of the breast (C50.-) is replaced by an Excludes1 instruction. This means coders need to pay close attention to the updated tabular instructions when D05.- and C50.- conditions appear in the same clinical scenario.

This is a good example of why simply downloading a list of "new codes" is not enough.

Some of the most important coding changes aren't brand-new code numbers. They are changes to coding instructions, inclusion terms, exclusion notes, sequencing, or code relationships.

A coder who reviews only the new-code list could easily miss an instruction change that affects actual claim reporting.

3. More Changes Mean More Pressure on Documentation

Every annual ICD-10 update eventually leads back to the same issue:

Can the medical record support the code being reported?

The FY 2027 official guidelines emphasize the importance of complete and accurate documentation and the collaboration between healthcare providers and coders.

That means coding education should not stop with the coding department.

Providers should also understand where documentation needs to be more specific.

For example, if a new code requires a particular anatomical site or clinical distinction, the provider needs to document that information clearly enough for the coder to assign the appropriate code.

This is especially important for high-volume diagnoses.

Instead of trying to train everyone on every single change, practices can start by identifying the diagnoses that appear most frequently in their own claims and reviewing how the FY 2027 update affects them.

4. Don't Forget ICD-10-PCS and MS-DRG Changes

For hospitals and inpatient coding teams, the October update also brings changes to ICD-10-PCS and MS-DRG classification.

CMS has published the FY 2027 ICD-10-PCS files, which apply to inpatient discharges from October 1, 2026 through March 31, 2027.

The FY 2027 PCS update includes 103 new codes, 3 revised titles, and 38 deleted codes, according to CMS's update summary.

At the same time, MS-DRG Version 44.0 is part of the FY 2027 update environment. CMS has published the Version 44 definitions and related materials.

For inpatient organizations, this creates another important implementation task:

Don't update the code tables while leaving your grouper and related systems behind.

Coding, grouping, reimbursement, and reporting workflows need to be tested together.

5. Telehealth and Other Payment Rules Need Separate Attention

One area that often causes confusion is the assumption that an ICD-10 update automatically creates or changes every telehealth billing rule.

It doesn't.

ICD-10-CM diagnosis coding and telehealth billing requirements involve different coding and payment components, including CPT/HCPCS codes, modifiers, place-of-service rules, payer policies, and Medicare instructions.

CMS continues to publish separate Medicare guidance affecting telehealth services, including billing instructions for specific provider settings.

So rather than simply telling coders to "use new telehealth diagnosis codes," practices should review their complete workflow:

documentation → diagnosis coding → CPT/HCPCS → modifier/POS → payer requirements → claim submission.

That approach reduces the risk of treating one coding update as if it changes the entire billing process.

Why Waiting Until September Is a Bad Strategy

The biggest mistake organizations can make is treating October 1 as the day they start preparing.

October 1 should be the day your updated workflow is already working.

CMS has made the FY 2027 files available, including the code tables, addendum, conversion table, and official coding guidelines.

That gives organizations time to:

  • Review new and deleted codes
  • Identify high-volume diagnoses affected by the update
  • Update EHR and encoder systems
  • Review documentation requirements
  • Update internal coding references
  • Train coding and CDI teams
  • Educate providers where documentation changes are needed
  • Test claims before the effective date

This is where coding and revenue cycle management overlap.

A code change that isn't loaded correctly into your systems can become a claim-edit problem.

A documentation issue can become a coding query.

A coding error can become a denial.

And a denial eventually becomes a cash-flow problem.

Your FY 2027 ICD-10 Preparation Checklist

Instead of trying to review the entire code set at once, use a structured approach.

1. Review Your Most Frequently Used Codes

Pull your top 25–50 diagnosis codes from recent claims.

Check each one against the FY 2027 code set.

Look specifically for:

  • Deleted codes
  • New replacement codes
  • Revised titles
  • New Excludes notes
  • Changes in specificity
  • New documentation requirements

2. Update Your Technology

Confirm that your:

  • EHR
  • Encoder
  • Practice management system
  • Claim-scrubbing software
  • Clearinghouse
  • CDI tools
  • Coding reference tools

are ready for the FY 2027 code set.

Don't assume that one software update automatically updates every downstream system.

3. Review Documentation With Providers

This step is often overlooked.

If a new or revised code requires greater specificity, make sure providers know what information needs to appear in the medical record.

A short provider education session can prevent weeks of coding queries and claim corrections later.

4. Test High-Volume Claims Before October 1

Don't wait for your first real claim to discover a problem.

Use your testing or sandbox environment to run representative claims using the new code set.

Pay particular attention to diagnoses that are:

  • High volume
  • High dollar
  • Frequently denied
  • Connected to medical necessity policies
  • Used in prior authorization workflows

5. Review Payer-Specific Requirements

An ICD-10 code may be valid, but that does not automatically mean every payer will process it in exactly the same way.

Review payer policies, medical necessity requirements, NCD/LCD changes, and authorization rules where applicable.

CMS has already issued FY 2027-related ICD-10 changes affecting certain Medicare coverage policies, including updates relevant to areas such as mammography and PET coverage.

How Medical Coding Services Can Help

For smaller practices and growing healthcare organizations, keeping up with annual coding changes can put additional pressure on already-busy billing and administrative teams.

That's where an experienced coding partner can provide additional support.

A strong coding workflow should go beyond simply assigning diagnosis codes. It should connect documentation review, coding accuracy, compliance, claim quality, and denial prevention.

If your organization needs additional support with annual updates, audits, documentation review, and day-to-day coding operations, our Medical Coding Services can help your team stay aligned with the latest coding requirements while keeping the broader revenue cycle in view.

The objective isn't to outsource responsibility.

It's to make sure your internal team has the expertise, processes, and quality controls needed to handle changes accurately.

The October 1 Deadline Should Not Be a Surprise

Every year, ICD-10 changes create the same temptation: wait until the deadline gets close, download the update, and start learning.

That approach puts unnecessary pressure on coders and providers.

The better approach is to treat the annual ICD-10 update as part of your revenue integrity calendar.

Review the codes.

Review the documentation.

Update the systems.

Test the claims.

Train the people.

Then go live.

Because in modern healthcare revenue cycle management, denial prevention starts much earlier than the billing office.

It starts with accurate documentation and the right code on the claim.

October 1, 2026 is the deadline. Your preparation should start well before it.

title: CAQH Updates: Every Provider Must Know
excerpt: Recent CAQH ProView changes that affect provider enrollment and credentialing timelines.
content:
CAQH has updated their verification process. Providers must update their profiles to avoid enrollment delays.

What's Changed

The new CAQH ProView 3.0 requires additional documentation and more frequent re-attestation. Non-compliance can result in enrollment suspensions.

Action Items

  • Log in to CAQH ProView and update your profile
  • Upload current insurance certificates
  • Re-attest to all existing attestations
